title: Bring People Along With Your Thinking
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses a common failure mode among leaders and experts: announcing a conclusion without walking others through the reasoning that produced it. The author argues that team members can't genuinely embrace a decision they haven't worked through themselves, so skipping the reasoning steps breeds confusion or quiet resistance rather than buy-in. The piece compares accepting an unexplained decision to eating a dish without knowing the ingredients — people approach it with suspicion. It recommends that leaders either retrace the premises that led to their conclusion or, better still, involve the team in the thinking process before the conclusion is reached. The underlying point is that execution depends less on the quality of a decision than on whether the team understands and accepts how it was reached.
points: Leaders who announce conclusions without explaining their reasoning often lose the team's understanding and buy-in.
Team members resist decisions they haven't been able to reach for themselves through discussion.
Skipping the thinking steps is often discovered only after implementation stalls or team members push back.
Retracing the premises accepted or rejected helps others appreciate the decision even if they still disagree.
The strongest approach is including the team in the thinking process before the conclusion is settled.
quotes: Leaders and experts who communicate excitement and conviction about their conclusions without describing how they got there end up losing people.
They won’t believe in any conclusion they haven’t reached for themselves through discussion and examination.
For talented team members, accepting a decision without understanding where it comes from is akin to eating a dish without knowing what is in it.
In their impatience to move to execution, they can jump ahead of the team and presume everyone gets it when they don’t.
A decision is the spark that ignites action. But only when the team accepts how the decision was made.
Bringing them along with their thinking is what good leaders do. Anything else is just getting ahead of your skis.
